Title: Rome in World Time, Part 6: The Augustan Peace and the Julio-Claudians (27 BC–AD 68)

Summary: Augustus turned a battered republic into a monarchy that pretended not to be one, and his family ruled for almost a century. It was called the Pax Romana, but it included the loss of three legions in Germany, a four-year revolt in the Balkans, army mutinies, Boudica's uprising in Britain, the Great Fire of Rome and the start of the Jewish revolt. In the same decades a usurper seized China's throne, Vietnam's Trưng sisters rose against Han, Buddhism reached China, and a Kushite queen fought Rome to a draw.

---

Augustus never called himself king or emperor in the modern sense. He was *princeps*, "first citizen," and he kept the Senate, the consuls and the elections. Real power sat with him because he controlled the army, the treasury of Egypt and the key provinces. The system he built, the **Principate**, lasted about 300 years.

## Augustus (27 BC–AD 14)

### Conquest and frontier wars

| Years | Event |
|---|---|
| 26–19 BC | **Cantabrian Wars**: Augustus finally completes the conquest of Spain, 200 years after Rome first arrived. Agrippa crushes the last revolt in 19 BC |
| 25 BC | Galatia (central Anatolia) annexed |
| 26–24 BC | **Aelius Gallus** leads an expedition into Arabia (Yemen); it fails because of disease and bad guides |
| 25–21/20 BC | War with the kingdom of **Kush** (Meroë). Queen **Amanirenas** raids Roman Egypt and carries off statues of Augustus; Rome counterattacks; a treaty at Samos gives Kush favourable terms. A bronze head of Augustus was buried under a Meroitic temple step and found in 1910 |
| 20 BC | Parthia returns the standards lost at Carrhae, by diplomacy. Augustus celebrates it on coins and on the Prima Porta statue |
| 16–15 BC | Raetia and Noricum (the Alps, modern Switzerland and Austria) conquered by Tiberius and Drusus |
| 12–9 BC | Drusus campaigns across the Rhine to the Elbe; he dies after a fall from his horse in 9 BC |
| 12–9 BC | Pannonia (western Hungary) conquered |
| AD 6 | **Judaea** becomes a Roman province; the census of Quirinius sparks a revolt by **Judas of Galilee** |

### The Great Illyrian Revolt (AD 6–9)

Just as Tiberius was about to attack the Marcomannic king Maroboduus in Bohemia, the newly conquered peoples of Pannonia and Dalmatia rose under two leaders both named **Bato**. Suetonius called it the most serious foreign war since Hannibal. Rome needed fifteen legions and three years to put it down.

### Disaster in the Teutoburg Forest (AD 9)

Three days after the Balkan revolt ended, news arrived from Germany. **Arminius**, a German chief who held Roman citizenship and had served with the Roman army, led the governor **Varus** and three legions (the XVII, XVIII and XIX) into an ambush in the forests near Kalkriese. Roughly 15,000–20,000 soldiers died. Suetonius says Augustus banged his head against a door, shouting "Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!" Rome never again tried to hold Germany up to the Elbe, and those legion numbers were never used again.

### Plots inside Rome

- 23 or 22 BC: conspiracy of **Fannius Caepio and Murena**, executed.
- 2 BC: Augustus' only daughter **Julia** is exiled for adultery; her lovers were accused of plotting.
- AD 8: the poet **Ovid** is exiled to the Black Sea for "a poem and a mistake."

## Tiberius (14–37)

Augustus died on 19 August AD 14. Within weeks, the legions of **Pannonia** and the **Rhine** **mutinied**, demanding shorter service and better pay. The Rhine legions offered to make Germanicus emperor; he refused and restored order, partly by letting the soldiers kill their own ringleaders (Tacitus, *Annals* 1.16–49).

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 14–16 | Germanicus campaigns in Germany, visits the Teutoburg battlefield, buries the dead and recovers two eagles |
| 17–24 | **Tacfarinas**, a Numidian ex-auxiliary, leads a guerrilla war in North Africa |
| 19 | Germanicus dies in Syria, possibly poisoned |
| 21 | **Revolt of Florus and Sacrovir** among debt-ridden Gallic nobles |
| 26 | Tiberius retires to **Capri**; the Praetorian Prefect **Sejanus** runs Rome |
| 28 | The **Frisians** revolt over taxes in hides |
| c. 30 or 33 | **Jesus of Nazareth** is crucified in Jerusalem under the prefect Pontius Pilate (prefect 26–36) |
| 31 | Sejanus is arrested and executed; a purge follows |

## Caligula (37–41) and Claudius (41–54)

**Caligula** was popular at first, then erratic and cruel. His planned invasion of Britain ended with soldiers collecting seashells on the Channel coast (the meaning of this is disputed). He executed King **Ptolemy of Mauretania** in AD 40, which sparked a revolt there. A conspiracy of officers led by Gaius Gaetulicus failed in 39; a second one by Praetorian officers succeeded on 24 January 41. The Praetorians found his uncle **Claudius** hiding behind a curtain and made him emperor.

| Year | Under Claudius |
|---|---|
| 40–44 | Mauretania revolt put down; two new provinces |
| 42 | **Scribonianus**, governor of Dalmatia, rebels. His legions abandon him within five days |
| **43** | **Invasion of Britain** under Aulus Plautius; Claudius arrives for the capture of Camulodunum (Colchester) |
| 47–51 | **Caratacus** resists in Wales until he is betrayed and paraded in Rome, where his speech wins him a pardon |
| c. 49 | Claudius expels Jews from Rome over unrest "at the instigation of Chrestus" (Suetonius; may refer to early Christians) |
| 54 | Claudius dies, probably poisoned by his wife Agrippina to put her son Nero on the throne |

## Nero (54–68)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 58–63 | War with Parthia over **Armenia**. The general **Corbulo** wins, then another general surrenders at Rhandeia (62). The compromise: a Parthian prince rules Armenia but is crowned by Rome |
| 59 | Nero has his mother **Agrippina** murdered |
| **60/61** | **Boudica**, queen of the Iceni, leads a revolt after Roman officials flog her and assault her daughters. Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium are burned; Tacitus says 70,000 died. Governor Suetonius Paulinus defeats her |
| 62 | Earthquake damages Pompeii |
| **64** | **Great Fire of Rome** (from 18/19 July) burns much of the city for six days. Nero blames the **Christians** and executes many; tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in this persecution |
| 65 | **Pisonian conspiracy**: discovered; Seneca, Lucan and many others forced to die |
| 66 | Tiridates of Armenia is crowned in Rome. Nero tours Greece as a performer |
| **66** | **Great Jewish Revolt**: the Jerusalem garrison is massacred; the governor of Syria, Cestius Gallus, is ambushed at Beth Horon and loses a legion's worth of men |
| 67 | **Vespasian** is sent to crush the revolt; reconquers Galilee (the commander Josephus surrenders and later writes the history) |
| 68 | **Vindex**, governor in Gaul, revolts and backs **Galba** in Spain. Clodius Macer revolts in Africa and cuts the grain. The Senate declares Nero an enemy; he kills himself on 9 June 68 |

The dynasty of Augustus was finished, and as Tacitus put it, the "secret of empire" was out: emperors could be made somewhere other than Rome.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**AD 9 was a bad year for two empires.** In the same year Rome lost three legions in Germany, Wang Mang ended the Han dynasty (for 14 years) and founded his own Xin dynasty. Wang Mang's attempted land reforms (nationalising land, abolishing slave sales) sound strangely like the Gracchi.

**AD 40–43: rebellious queens and invasions at both ends of Eurasia.** The Trưng sisters drove out Han officials in Vietnam in 40 and were defeated in 43, the same year Claudius' legions landed in Britain. Eighteen years later Boudica would lead a similar revolt in Britain.

**Buddhism reached China as Nero died.** Traditional accounts put the White Horse Temple's founding in 68, the year of Nero's suicide. Christianity and Buddhism, two great missionary religions, were spreading along opposite ends of the same trade routes at the same time.

**A Japanese king and Nero's tutor in the same decade.** A gold seal sent from China to a king in Japan in 57 is one of the earliest securely dated objects linking Japan to written history. At the time, Seneca was running Rome for the young Nero.

**Romans almost reached the source of the Nile.** Nero's expedition, reported by Seneca and Pliny, went up the Nile beyond Meroë to the great swamps of South Sudan. It shows Rome and Kush were on working terms after the war under Augustus.

## What comes next

Part 7: the Year of the Four Emperors, the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, Vesuvius, the Colosseum, Trajan's conquests, Hadrian's Wall, the Bar Kokhba revolt and Marcus Aurelius' wars. Meanwhile, a Chinese envoy almost reaches Rome, paper is reported invented, and a "Roman embassy" turns up in Luoyang.

## Sources and notes

- Augustus, *Res Gestae Divi Augusti* (his own account, surviving as an inscription).
- Tacitus, *Annals* (Tiberius to Nero, with gaps); Tacitus, *Agricola* (Britain).
- Suetonius, *The Twelve Caesars*.
- Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, Books 53–63.
- Velleius Paterculus, *Roman History*, Book 2 (a contemporary who served under Tiberius in the Illyrian revolt).
- Josephus, *The Jewish War*.
- Ban Gu, *Han Shu*, and Fan Ye, *Hou Hanshu*, for Wang Mang, the Trưng sisters and the gold seal.
- Overview: [Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Teutoburg_Forest), [Boudica (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boudica), [Trưng sisters (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C6%B0ng_sisters), [Meroë Head (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mero%C3%AB_Head).

**Flags:** The year of Jesus' crucifixion (usually AD 30 or 33) and birth (c. 6–4 BC) are scholarly estimates. The traditional date for the White Horse Temple is not certain, and Buddhism likely reached China earlier through merchants. Kushan and Indo-Parthian reign dates are debated. Tacitus' casualty figure for Boudica's revolt is unverifiable. The Teutoburg death toll is an estimate based on the size of three legions plus auxiliaries.
